free_tier.stated: 'No-strings-attached prize money for talented builders, scientists, operators', distributed as '1st prize $100,000', '2nd prize $30,000', '3rd prize $20,000', '4th - 23rd $5,000 ea.', totalling '$250,000' across 23 winners. Eligibility is the widest found in this class, quoted: 'Anyone who builds things, discovers things, or does things ... There is no limit on age, interest, location, etc.' The conditions are removed explicitly: 'You can spend the money however you want. We take no equity and have zero expectations.' and 'What do I have to do if I win? Nothing!' The application 'is designed to take 5-10 minutes'. The cycle is complete and paid: the site now reads 'The winners have been selected.'

chaining: Cash with no spending restriction and no equity, so it composes with every other record: the USD 100,000 first prize is roughly 20 to 100 times the largest compute credit in this corpus and can be spent at spot or marketplace rates the recipient chooses. notes: The best-evidenced award in this class and the one to promote first, because payment is not a claim but a published list of 23 named people with amounts beside them. Two properties make it stronger than the Open Intelligence Foundation offer: the terms name the removals explicitly ('no equity', 'zero expectations', 'nothing' required after winning), and one winner is observably outside the United States and unaffiliated. The failure mode is that the cycle is closed and the programme is three individuals, not an institution: the prize pool is described as money they pooled, the site is a static page, and the winners page closes with 'See you next time' rather than a date. So the finding is a closed cycle worth watching for the next one, not an open door. A recurring cadence is implied by 'See you next time' and by the Duct Tape Prize predecessor, and by a 'Remind me. We'll email you near the deadline' control, but no next-round date was published on any page read today, so treat recurrence as likely rather than promised.
